thread.title: Vail Resorts: Moving The Mountain In The Right Direction - Vail Resorts, Inc. (NYSE:MTN)

author: StrategyDoc
title: Vail Resorts: Moving The Mountain In The Right Direction - Vail Resorts, Inc. (NYSE:MTN)
text:
Background The business of ski resorts today is fundamentally different from the old resorts of the 1960s through 1990s. Gone are the days when the wildcat owner could find a snowy winter location, buy the land cheaply or sign a lease (usually with the US Forest Service), clear some trees, build a small base area, and let nature do its thing in winter… snow.
While challenging enough, today the ski resort business is about more than hoping the weather will cooperate. It includes the need to provide better, more adaptive customer experiences; an organizational emphasis on speed, quality, and productivity in delivering customer needs; more emphasis on employee empowerment and self-direction that allow more responsive guest services; a focus on core processes that deliver a better guest experience; a leaner, more streamlined organizational structure that removes needless costs; a shift from management to leadership orientation, with a focus on high-performance teams delivering positive guest experiences; a greater application of technologies and knowledge to create enhanced customer value; an additional focus on partnerships and alliances to expand customer appeal and revenue generation.
Recognizing these challenges requires putting capital in play and, over the past decade, Vail Resorts ( MTN ) has an industry-leading track record of reinvestment ; with more than $1.2 billion invested in ways that improve guest experiences and, with it, a pronounced desire to return to a Vail Resort.
However, merely investing in a business does not ensure success if that business does not recognize certain realities.
Vail Business Strategies While not to conflate industries, it is instructive to look at Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) and the years 1993-1997 when it was at the brink of failure - as it found itself struggling for a consistently profitable source of revenue, trying and failing to market everything from digital cameras to portable CD players to TV appliances. It was then that Steve Jobs was ousted due to internal squabbles and the company suffered through a revolving door of stopgap CEOs. Finally, in 1997, Jobs returned as CEO and instituted a bold change in strategies that led to the iPod, the iPad, and, of course, the iPhone; not to mention the Apple Stores that were a business line extension that offered the means to sell and service Apple products directly.
This was a clear change in strategic direction borne of innovating the business model. The need for business model innovation was recognized in the 2011 research by the Economist Intelligence Unit, which surveyed more than 4,000 business managers and found that 54% believed that business model innovation was more important for success than product or service innovation. This was eye-opening for many because to accomplish a business model change required creating strategies aligned with a basic question…“What different sources of revenue are available to us, and could we build a business with a radically different mix?”
While we have certainly seen the business model innovation from Apple, it is a rarity as few companies are willing or able to alter their business model. However, upon closer inspection, that appears to be what Vail Resorts is doing, in its effort to offer a compelling year-round attraction to its customers who, with an average income of more than $150,000 per year, have money to spend.
The three strategies upon which Vail’s business model is based include the following:
The Mountain Strategy:
This strategy involves continuous reinvestment in the resorts to maintain a ski leadership position, with both capital investments on the mountains (snowmaking and run grooming) and by redeveloping the base areas and adding new lodging and amenities.
In addition to selling lift tickets, it also drives the growth of ancillary businesses, including the ski school, retail, equipment rental and dining, the combination of which comprises more than half of its mountain revenue. The emphasis is on controlling its fixed cost structure and better flow through revenue growth, with increased operating margins.
An essential part of its mountain strategy includes what Vail calls “opportunistic” acquisitions that add to its portfolio of resorts in existing geographic areas, or by adding new resorts or complimentary businesses in new geographic areas.
The mountain strategy is focused on how to complement its business model with new venues that can be effectively integrated and offer ancillary growth; as with “premier” mountain areas in North America, Australia, and Asia.
The Lodging Strategy:
This builds on the Mountain Strategy because it involves the selective expansion of its luxury RockResorts by leveraging its expertise across the Vail Resorts network. RockResorts was founded in 1956 by Laurance Rockefeller and has a history of managing legendary hotels and resort properties. Acquired by Vail in 2001, it is being used to help with the design, marketing, sales and management of planned new developments, as it combines expertise in real estate development and resort management, all while leveraging its strong brands with its well-identified customers.
The primary strategy in Lodging is to ensure Vail provides a high-quality, comprehensive experience by controlling thousands of beds at the foot of its mountain resorts. The company does this in two ways: through the ownership of several hotels, and the management of hotels and condominium properties across its resorts. Both are carefully selected to offer a wide variety of lodging experiences to meet the varying needs of guests.
The Real Estate Strategy:
While focused on the core business – operations of resorts and base areas – Vail has shifted away from being the sole developer of real estate projects. Instead of developing prime parcels of Vail Resorts land by itself, Vail is looking for geographically focused and capable third-party partners to lend its expertise in development, so as to work with specific communities and governments. While no small challenge, there is a significant benefit in having the local knowledge and relationships brought to bear on economic development, including the expansion of property management and commercial leasing to bring in dining and retail to fully realize the revenue potential.
Innovating to Compete in a Changing Environment Prior to the Great Recession, the ski resort business was largely fragmented, one in which individual or small groups of resorts dominated the industry. While the barriers to entry required specific access to locations with the requisite geography/topography/climate, we saw resorts opened by a range of people, usually those with a passion for skiing rather than skills in operating a business. And, this may provide reason for the hand-to-mouth existence we have seen at some resorts; many where a bad snow season could mean closing. And, closings there have been.
In 1990, there were 569 ski resorts operating in the US. When the 2018-2019 ski season opened, there were 472 ski resorts in operation, roughly a 17% reduction in the number of resorts, with many more on economic life support. And, while the ski resort industry might like to believe it is different from other industries, it is not. It is subject to the same vagaries of the industry life-cycle as other businesses.
This suggests a ski industry where the choices are less about location or cost and more about what experiences the well-identified customer might receive for their time and money. As is typical in all businesses that face a change in the competitive environment, we see consolidation through M&A and this is exactly what we are seeing. As is typical, the bigger players dominate, not only as with Vail but with privately held Alterra Mountain .
While Vail owns and operates 19 resorts in three countries and has ski pass partnerships that offer access to 46 resorts, principally in Europe, Japan, and Canada, Alterra Mountain is joining Vail in the effort to reach more customers (generally those with greater sums of disposal income). Correspondingly, Alterra Mountain now owns 14 destinations and has ski pass partnerships with 38 ski destinations; again, many differentiated enough to attract a premium price.
Whether through acquisitions or partnerships , the benefits of scale for the ski industry are notable because they usually result in improving the company’s financial performance, removing excess capacity from the industry (as evident with closing of 17% of US ski resorts since 1990), and accelerated access to products that appeal through differentiation. M&A is valuable because it also allows access to a developed location faster and cheaper than if built from scratch (which also serves to appeal to skier loyalty and that translates into repeat visits).
Again, whether through acquisitions or partnerships, economies of scale allow Vail buyer power (e.g., the purchasing of critical technology and equipment less expensively). This improves the ability to provide customers with a unique experience at multiple sites and that moves the business from a cost focus to that of differentiation, where customers are willing to pay a premium (higher price) for the product.
Differentiation is also evident in the technology that is changing the ski industry in many positive ways, and is another source of innovation for Vail Resorts, that is effectively delivering on customer needs. It is also where we see Vail investing. For example, we see the operational value of an investment in Artificial Intelligence that is serving the Vail customer.
“Emma” is the world's first digital mountain assistant and Vail is employing it to guide guests at nine Vail Resort properties through text messaging. “Emma” will spend the rest of the 2018-19 ski season in beta and will get smarter the more she interacts with guests and expands her knowledge base and insight. By texting 77477, the guest will hear, "I am the collective knowledge of every lift operator, groomer, snowmaker, ski school instructor, ticket counter attendant and ski patroller," says Emma. "I can help you with weather, lift status, terrain, parking, traffic, shuttles, rentals, lessons, lift tickets, resort experiences, planning and more – just ask!"
The investment in Artificial Intelligence establishes a higher level of differentiation that appeals to the skier/snowboarder on the mountain and is another example of how Vail invests to differentiate.
Summary Over various years I have had occasion to visit ten ski resorts operated by Vail. However, as skiing injuries have put my aggressive skiing days behind me, I have become more appreciative of the ski resorts that offer not only challenging slopes but also nice lodging, fine dining, and other outdoor or indoor activities that transcend the obvious reliance on ski-worthy snow. This is an important point, as the future for ski resorts is not merely how to entice more skiers and snowboarders to the mountain in the pursuit of an “Endless Winter." Rather, in countering the cyclical nature of the ski business and its reliance on weather, topography and geography, the future business success of ski resorts will lie in a highly differentiated business that goes beyond the mountain and is enhanced by the synergistic nature of the investments in not only the Mountain, but in Lodging and Real Estate Development. It is Vail’s adaptive business model that is enabling it to utilize its sunk cost assets more fully by reimagining the snow-focused activities at its ski resorts into a year-round revenue opportunity that turns the pursuit of “Endless Winter” into “Endless Enjoyment.”
What will drive the continued consolidation of the ski industry will not be better skiing, snowboarding, or even snowshoeing opportunities. It will be the investments that attract people to the ski areas for year-round activities that include such activities as golf , mountain biking , running and hiking trails , ziplines , scenic gondola/lift rides to the top of the mountain, water parks , Alpine slides , and, of course, the ubiquitous game arcades. (Go ahead and click on the words, it is a fun world to visit...online and in person.)
While none of it comes cheaply, it is the means to attract people for reasons beyond having sufficient snow to slide on. It will be about fun opportunities that provide Endless Enjoyment! This is the level of differentiation needed for the ski resorts of the future, and that is the direction Vail Resorts is heading.
